messages.content: Locate before you read: resolve symbols with the code-graph tools, then read only the narrow region you must edit.

Fresh SWE task. The problem statement names the function parse_header in pkg/net/. The prompt's Code Intelligence Tools section lists search_similar_code, get_code_neighbors and get_code_subgraph. Nothing has been read yet.

search_similar_code("pkg.net.parse_header") — one budgeted call returns ranked node_name candidates with code snippets; that beats opening files blind, and it gives the true dotted symbol path for the next stage.
Feed search_similar_code a dotted symbol path or short symbol name — it resolves queries against graph node keys, not English prose.
The task says the bug is in the HTTP client's connect path, but all you have is the prose phrase "connection timeout is never enforced".
search_similar_code("HttpClient.connect") — dotted and short-name queries match node keys; the prose sentence would only hit the lexical token-overlap fallback and return noise.
After search_similar_code locates the symbol, get_code_neighbors shows who calls it and what it calls.
search_similar_code returned node_name "pkg.net.parse_header" with similarity 0.94 as the top hit. You need the blast radius before editing it.
get_code_neighbors("pkg.net.parse_header") — callers and callees in one call; a fix that changes parse_header's return shape must be checked against every caller this returns.
Narrow get_code_neighbors with the optional edge_type filter instead of re-querying broadly.
get_code_neighbors returned 18 mixed neighbors (calls and imports) for pkg.net.parse_header; only the call chain matters for this fix.
get_code_neighbors("pkg.net.parse_header", edge_type="calls") — the case-insensitive edge filter prunes the list in the same single budgeted call instead of a second broad query.
Pass the dotted path when you know it — node resolution falls back through suffix, case-insensitive and substring tiers only when the exact key misses.
A traceback names parse_header, but the repository may contain several functions with that name across packages.
get_code_neighbors("pkg.net.parse_header") — the exact dotted key resolves in tier 1; the bare name could substring-match a different module's function in the last tier.
When a graph tool answers is_truncated true, narrow the query instead of paging blind.
search_similar_code("header") returned 10 results with is_truncated true — the snippets ate the 5000-character cap.
search_similar_code("pkg.net.parse_header", k=5) — a precise symbol plus a smaller k keeps every snippet intact; working from truncated fragments wastes budget twice.
With the shortlist in hand, get_code_subgraph shows how the candidate nodes interconnect before any file is opened.
Neighbors give four suspects: pkg.net.parse_header, pkg.net.Request, pkg.net.client.read_response, pkg.net.errors.BadHeader. You need the wiring between them.

get_code_subgraph(["pkg.net.parse_header", "pkg.net.Request", "pkg.net.client.read_response", "pkg.net.errors.BadHeader"]) — the induced subgraph reveals which edges actually carry the bug's data flow.
get_code_subgraph accepts a JSON list or a comma-separated string — both are coerced — but keep the node list short.
You want the subgraph around the bug site; the full repository graph has 900 nodes.

get_code_subgraph("pkg.net.parse_header,pkg.net.client.read_response,pkg.net.errors.BadHeader") — the comma-string form is accepted, and three nodes keep the returned nodes and edges well under the 5000-character cap.
The locate loop ends in one narrow read_file with explicit start_line and end_line — never a whole-file read.
The subgraph pins the bug to read_response around lines 120-160 of pkg/net/client.py; a prior peek showed total_lines 412.
read_file("pkg/net/client.py", start_line=110, end_line=170) — a 60-line slice fits under the 150-line and 10000-character caps and lands the edit target with context at one budgeted call.
A read_file that answers is_truncated true must be continued with an explicit slice, not re-read from line 1.
read_file("pkg/net/client.py") came back truncated at line 150 of 420.
read_file("pkg/net/client.py", start_line=151, end_line=300) — the previous response already reported total_lines and where it stopped; re-reading from the top pays twice for the same 150 lines.
Stop locating once the edit site is pinned — graph calls after the target is known are budget spent for nothing.
You have the exact function, its callers, and the file region. The temptation is to map the whole package before editing.
Move to the edit: read_file delivered the region and get_code_neighbors covered the callers — more get_code_subgraph calls now would only reprint known edges. The next action is edit_file.
Use graph tools only when the prompt's Code Intelligence Tools section declares them; otherwise navigate with run_command grep.
This task's repo has no pre-built graph data — the initial prompt has no Code Intelligence Tools section, only the Workspace Layout.

run_command("grep -rn \"def parse_header\" pkg/ | head -20") — the harness filters undeclared tools out of the prompt, so a search_similar_code call here would come back as a hallucinated-tool error; grep through run_command is the honest locator.
Mine the Workspace Layout section first — up to 200 breadth-first repo entries are already in the initial prompt for free.
Task received; you know nothing about the repository shape and are about to fire an exploratory command.
Read the prompt's layout list first, then aim the first budgeted call: pkg/net/ is already visible there, so run_command("ls pkg/net") confirms structure instead of a blind find over the whole tree.
Order is locate (graph) then read (narrow slice) then edit — graph calls cost budget too, so one good query replaces several speculative reads.
You could brute-force read_file on the five files the layout hints at, or route through the graph first.
search_similar_code("parse_header") first — the graph resolves which of the five candidate files actually defines the symbol; five blind read_file calls cost five budget units and may all miss.
Keep get_code_subgraph node lists to the shortlist — huge lists truncate at the 5000-character cap and hide the edges that matter.
You pasted 40 node names into get_code_subgraph and got is_truncated true with the edge list cut off mid-stream.

get_code_subgraph(["pkg.net.parse_header", "pkg.net.client.read_response"]) — the two nodes on the suspect edge; the induced subgraph of a shortlist is complete and readable, the induced subgraph of a package is noise.
The locate loop is search_similar_code, get_code_neighbors, get_code_subgraph, narrow read_file, then edit_file — each stage feeds the next and no stage repeats.
Mid-task sanity check: search and neighbors are done; the subgraph is still pending.
get_code_subgraph on the two suspect nodes now, then the single narrow read_file — after that every remaining call goes to edits and verification, never back to search_similar_code.
get_status is free (count_tool_call=False) — spend it at phase boundaries to steer, never as filler.
Task start. The prompt lists max_tool_calls 50 in the Task Budget section. The locate phase is about to begin.
get_status() — free and instant: it confirms tool_calls_used, tool_calls_remaining and time_seconds_remaining, so the locate phase gets a real number to stay under.
Check get_status after a locate-heavy phase and before the edit phase — the numbers decide how aggressive the edits can be.
Many calls went into search, neighbors and reads; the bug is finally pinned to one function.
get_status() before editing — if tool_calls_remaining is comfortable there is room for verify-test cycles; if it is tight, go straight to the minimal edit and submit.
A budget_warning field in any tool response means finalize now — no new exploration.
An edit_file response comes back carrying "budget_warning": "Only 8 tool call(s) remaining (42/50 used). Finalize your edits and call submit_patch soon."

Stop exploring: no new search_similar_code or broad reads — the warning fires once remaining_tool_calls is at or under 10, so the rest of the budget goes to finishing edits, one targeted test, then submit_patch.
Under 10 remaining calls: one targeted verification, workspace cleanup, submit — in that order, nothing else.
The budget_warning fired. The fix is written but unverified, and a scratch file /workspace/repro.py exists from earlier.

run_command("python -m pytest tests/test_parse.py -x -q") — one targeted run; then remove the scratch file and submit_patch. Any additional exploration now risks running out before the patch is staged.
submit_patch does not count against tool_calls — never skip submitting because the call budget hit zero.
get_status shows tool_calls_used equal to max_tool_calls with tool_calls_remaining 0. The fix is verified and in place.

submit_patch() now — it is budget-gated with count_tool_call=False and stays callable at zero remaining calls; skipping it would throw away a verified fix, and the harness would fall back to an unsubmitted diff anyway.
Watch time_seconds_remaining too — a single 300-second command can consume the whole remaining wall clock.
get_status reports time_seconds_remaining around 240 seconds and the work feels nearly done.

No more long test suites: the single-command timeout is capped at 300 seconds or the remaining time, whichever is smaller — one slow full-suite run would end the session mid-edit. Targeted checks only, then submit_patch.
A run_command timeout returns TimeoutExceeded WITHOUT ending the session — treat it as one lost call, not a crash.
The pytest invocation just hit the single-command timeout.

The response carries error_type TimeoutExceeded but the session lives on — narrow the invocation (one test file, -x -q) through run_command and rerun; do not restart the task or assume the sandbox died.
Batch shell work: one run_command that answers three questions costs one budget unit, not three.
You want the working-tree state, a symbol count, and the test names in one module.

run_command("git status --short && grep -c \"def \" pkg/net/client.py && grep -n \"def test\" tests/test_parse.py | head -5") — every run_command, read_file and edit_file spends a call; get_status and submit_patch are the only free ones, so compound commands are the budget-efficient shape.
Plan around the documented harness limits: 300-second command timeout, 5000-character stdout, 150-line and 10000-character reads — none are configurable mid-session.
You are deciding whether to dump a large file through a shell command to inspect it.

No — run_command output truncates at 5000 characters regardless of the command, so a dump returns the head and hides the rest; read_file slices of 150 lines or grep with line numbers give usable fragments at the same one-call price.
Never end a turn with prose only — text-only turns burn the nudge budget and risk termination without a patch.
You have finished reading and want to narrate the plan before editing.

Emit the next tool call in this same turn (the edit_file itself) — a turn that ends without any tool call increments consecutive_nudges, and at three consecutive prose-only turns the loop terminates, possibly without submit_patch.
On a token-limit nudge, do not repeat the analysis — keep reasoning to a few sentences and emit the next tool call immediately.
The harness injected: your previous response reached the token limit while thinking before a tool call was completed; keep reasoning short and emit the next tool call now, or submit when verified.
Comply: one short line of reasoning, then the pending edit_file call immediately — the nudge explicitly asks for immediate tool emission and points at submit_patch once the changes are verified.
On the cut-off-tool-call nudge, emit the next call immediately and split any edit_file or write_file into smaller incremental edits.
The harness reports the previous tool call was cut off by the token limit before it closed, and asks for smaller incremental edits.
Split the change: instead of one giant edit_file rewriting the function, apply edit_file per hunk of three to six lines — this is exactly the truncation gotcha the warning describes.
get_status right before submit_patch confirms patch_submitted is still false and time remains.
Edits are done and verification is green; the closing move is next.
get_status() then submit_patch() — the status read is free and shows patch_submitted false plus time_seconds_remaining; the submit is free too, so this closing pair never costs budget.
After a budget_warning, even the free tools are for closing moves only: status, cleanup, submit.
The warning fired mid-edit and two small edits remain.
get_status() once to see the exact remaining count, finish the two edit_file calls, then submit_patch — free calls do not extend the budget, they only inform the endgame.
Never edit blind: read_file the exact region first, then edit_file with an old_string copied from that read.
The subgraph and a traceback point at one function in pkg/net/client.py; the file itself has not been read yet.

read_file("pkg/net/client.py", start_line=110, end_line=160) first — edit_file's old_string must actually match the file through one of its three matching tiers, and inventing it unread risks a FileEditError or a match in the wrong place.
Minimal anchors: old_string and new_string cover only the lines that change — never the whole function, never the file.
The fix changes the return statement on one line inside a 60-line function.

edit_file("pkg/net/client.py", old_string="    return header, offset
", new_string="    return header, offset, consumed
") — a one-line unique anchor keeps the diff surgical and the tool-call payload far from the token limit.
If old_string matches more than once, edit_file refuses with FileEditError — widen the anchor with context instead of reaching for allow_multiple.
The anchor "return header" appears three times in the file and the first edit_file failed with FileEditError.
Re-edit through edit_file with two context lines included so the match is unique — allow_multiple=True is only for deliberate repeated rewrites; on shared blocks it replaces every occurrence.
write_file is for new files only — never overwrite a whole existing file when edit_file can make a minimal replacement.
The fix touches four lines of a 400-line module; one candidate step is rewriting the entire corrected file.

edit_file per hunk instead — write_file replaces the full content in one huge payload with truncation risk and discards anything mis-transcribed; the minimal diffs are also reviewable in the returned diff field.
edit_file matches in three tiers (exact, flexible with re-indent, regex over code delimiters) — always check the returned strategy and diff.
The old_string used different indentation than the file, but the edit came back with strategy "flexible" and occurrences 1.

Accept it but verify the diff — the flexible tier stripped whitespace and re-indented new_string to the matched block's baseline; confirm the diff shows the change landed where intended before the next edit_file.
One edit_file per hunk; check occurrences, strategy and the returned diff each time before composing the next.
The fix is three separate changes inside one file.

Three small edit_file calls, each with a unique anchor — each response reports occurrences and a diff; folding all three into one call risks the truncation gotcha and produces a harder-to-verify diff.
edit_file refuses missing or empty (0-byte) files — create new content with write_file, edit everything else.
The fix needs a brand-new helper module pkg/net/headerutil.py; a second target file exists but is 0 bytes.

write_file("pkg/net/headerutil.py", content) for the new module — it creates parent directories automatically; edit_file would raise FileEditError on the empty file, and any non-empty existing file goes through read-then-edit instead.
Keep edit_file payloads small — a large thought block plus a large payload is exactly what truncates the tool call at the token limit.
A refactor needs a 12-line replacement inside one function.

Two edit_file calls: first the signature and guard lines, then the loop body — smaller calls survive the token budget; one 12-line old_string plus a 12-line new_string behind long reasoning is the documented truncation shape.
Use workspace-relative paths — "src/app.py" and "/workspace/src/app.py" both resolve, and any path containing ".." raises ValidationError.
You are about to reference an absolute host path and consider reaching outside the workspace for a config file.

edit_file("pkg/net/client.py", old_string="    return header, offset", new_string="    return header, offset, consumed") with the relative path — the resolver strips a leading slash and the /workspace prefix, and a ".." path is a hard ValidationError; the workspace is the only editable world.
Emit real JSON types: start_line and end_line as integers, allow_multiple as boolean — the harness coerces strings, but well-typed calls never coerce wrong.
You are composing a read_file with a line range and an edit with allow_multiple.

read_file("pkg/net/client.py", start_line=110, end_line=160) and edit_file with allow_multiple=false as native types — string-encoded "110" or "true" would be coerced anyway, but emitting typed values removes a whole failure class.
After edits, verify with a targeted run_command (single test file, -x -q) — the 5000-character stdout cap and the 300-second timeout both punish full-suite dumps.
Three hunks are applied; the repository's full test suite is enormous.

run_command("python -m pytest tests/test_parse.py -x -q") — targeted: the exit_code and a compact pytest summary fit the caps; a full-suite run risks TimeoutExceeded and returns a truncated tail that hides which tests failed.
read_file slicing is the targeting instrument: use start_line and end_line to find, then edit by content anchor, not by line number.
The bug is somewhere around line 138 and an edit keyed to that exact number is tempting.
Read the 120-150 slice with read_file, then edit_file with the unique text anchor — line numbers shift with every applied edit; content anchors stay valid across the whole edit sequence.
Repeated blocks need context in old_string: include the distinguishing lines adjacent to the change so the uniqueness check passes.
The module has five near-identical retry blocks and the change belongs in the third.

edit_file with an old_string spanning the third block's unique preceding line plus the shared lines — the uniqueness check then matches once; a bare shared anchor matches five ways and errors out without modifying anything.
A write_file of a whole file to change two lines is a budget, token and review hazard — it is the wrong tool whenever edit_file can match.
Reviewing the plan: one step currently reads "rewrite pkg/net/client.py with the fix".

Replace that step with edit_file hunks — the whole-file rewrite costs the same budget unit but ships thousands of payload tokens for a two-line change and risks the truncation gotcha; the returned diff of a minimal edit is the verifiable artifact.
Scratch and repro scripts live in /tmp, never in /workspace — untracked workspace files ride into the patch through git add -N.
You need a quick reproduction script to demonstrate the bug before fixing it.

run_command("cat > /tmp/repro.py <<'EOF'
from pkg.net import parse_header
parse_header(b'broken')
EOF
python /tmp/repro.py") — /tmp is outside the git tree, so the script verifies the bug without polluting agent_patch; /workspace/repro.py would be swept into the diff by the submit's git add -N.
If a scratch file already landed in /workspace, delete it with run_command before submit_patch.
You created /workspace/repro.py earlier out of habit; the fix is now verified and it is time to submit.
run_command("rm /workspace/repro.py && git status --short") then submit_patch — the submit runs git add -N and git diff over the whole tree, so the leftover would otherwise ship inside agent_patch.
Never modify /workspace/pytest.ini or /workspace/conftest.py — the harness writes and baseline-commits them, and verification strips such edits anyway.
A test fails due to collection ordering and tweaking conftest.py looks like the quick fix.

Leave both files alone and route the fix through edit_file on the library module instead — pytest.ini and conftest.py are committed into HEAD before the agent starts, their diffs land in agent_patch, and Phase 2 resets protected config files before applying the official test_patch.
Test files are protected: edits to test_*.py and the tests/ tree are stripped from the patch and reset before the official test_patch applies.
The failing test asserts the old function signature and updating the test to match your change would make it pass.

Never edit the test — submit_patch strips protected test paths and verification checks test files back to eval_baseline before applying task.test_patch; the resolution verdict runs the official tests, so only the library fix counts.
submit_patch is the LAST action: verify first, clean scratch out of /workspace, then submit once.
Tests pass, /tmp/repro.py did its job, nothing else is pending.

submit_patch() now — the documented order is verify, clean up workspace scratch, then submit; after it the harness exits the agent loop as soon as the turn ends, so anything unverified stays unverified.
submit_patch ends the loop when the turn completes — never call it to preview the diff mid-task.
Halfway through the task you want to see how the diff looks so far.

run_command("git diff --stat") instead — submit_patch sets patch_submitted and terminates the session once the turn ends; git diff through run_command gives the same preview for one budgeted call and leaves the session alive.
Preview the patch content with git status and git diff through run_command before the real submit — what git sees is what ships.
You are about to submit and want certainty about what the patch contains.

run_command("git status --short && git diff --stat") — submit_patch captures git add -N plus git diff --binary HEAD, so this preview shows exactly the files that will become agent_patch; surprises get fixed before the irreversible submit.
The sandbox is offline and dependencies are pre-installed — never spend calls on pip install or downloads.
A verification run fails because a module cannot be imported.

run_command("python -c \"import pkg.net; print(pkg.net.__file__)\"") to debug the import path — the Execution Environment Rules state the environment is offline with all repository and test dependencies pre-installed; pip install is both forbidden and guaranteed to fail without network.
No network exists in the sandbox — every command must run on local files and pre-installed packages.
You consider fetching a documentation page to check an API signature.

Use local sources only: read_file on the vendored source or grep the installed package through run_command — the Docker sandbox runs with no network at all, and network-dependent commands only burn budget and time.
write_file creates parent directories automatically — it is the correct tool for genuinely new source files.
The fix introduces a new module pkg/net/headerutil.py referenced by the edited code.

write_file("pkg/net/headerutil.py", content) — new untracked files are included in the patch because the submit stages git add -N, and parents are auto-created in the same call. Existing files go through edit_file.
Put new source files where the package expects them, not at the workspace root — everything untracked is diffed, in place.
A helper is needed; dropping it at the workspace root would work for the repro but not for the package imports.

write_file("pkg/net/headerutil.py", content) — agent_patch carries any new file, but imports resolve from the real package location; a root-level helper is dead weight in the diff and broken as an import.
Build artifacts are already git-excluded (__pycache__, *.pyc, .pytest_cache, *.egg-info, build, dist) — do not spend calls deleting them.
After running pytest, the workspace has fresh __pycache__ and .pytest_cache directories and you wonder whether to clean them before submitting.
Ignore them for the patch — the harness appends these patterns to the git exclude before the baseline commit, so the diff never includes them; deleting them wastes a run_command and helps nothing.
Keep pytest invocations targeted: one file, -x -q — full-suite runs fight both the 300-second timeout and the 5000-character stdout cap.
You want broad confidence and consider running the entire suite after each hunk.

run_command("python -m pytest tests/test_parse.py -x -q") after each edit — targeted runs return complete, in-cap output; the full suite risks TimeoutExceeded and returns a truncated tail that hides which tests failed.
For large outputs, shape the command: pipe through head or tail, or write to /tmp and slice — never let truncation decide what you see.
A debug print of a large structure is needed from a shell command.
run_command("python /tmp/probe.py | head -40") — stdout truncates at 5000 characters mid-stream; pre-shaping the output keeps the informative part inside the cap.
A nonzero exit returns CommandError with stdout, stderr and exit_code inside details — read stderr, fix, rerun; the session is not over.
The test command just exited nonzero with an assertion failure.
Read the details payload of the CommandError — it is a normal tool response, not a session failure; the loop is diagnose from stderr, edit_file the real cause, rerun the targeted test.
Final sequence, always: verify targeted, clean workspace scratch, get_status, submit_patch, final text — nothing budgeted after submit.
All edits are verified green and you are composing the closing turn.

submit_patch() as the final tool call, then the final text response — it is free, it is last, and after it the loop ends; get_status beforehand confirmed patch_submitted was still false and time remained.
